questions.enonce_markdown:
Examine Paul's teaching on food offered to idols.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** In 1 Corinthians 8-10 Paul answers a question from the Corinthian church about meat that had been offered to idols. In a city full of pagan temples, meat from sacrifices was eaten at feasts in temples and also sold in the market. Christians were divided: some, who prided themselves on their "knowledge", said that idols are nothing and so the food was harmless, while others, with a "weak" conscience, were troubled when they ate it.

**1. The main principles of Paul's teaching.**
- *Knowledge and love (8:1-3).* "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up." Being right in theory is not enough if it harms others.
- *Idols are nothing (8:4-6).* For Christians there is only one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ. Idols have no real existence as gods, so the food in itself is not changed.
- *The weak conscience (8:7-13).* Not everyone has this knowledge. Some, who were used to idols, eat as though it were really offered to an idol, and their conscience is defiled. Food will not commend us to God (8:8), but the strong must not become a stumbling block to the weak. Paul says that he would never eat meat again if it caused his brother to fall (8:13).
- *Paul's example (ch. 9).* He gave up his rights as an apostle (to support, to marry) for the sake of the gospel, and becomes "all things to all people". The strong should follow his example of giving up freedom for others.
- *Warning from Israel's history (10:1-13).* The Israelites in the wilderness had privileges but fell into idolatry and were punished. Christians who think they stand should take care.
- *Flee from idolatry (10:14-22).* Taking part in meals in a pagan temple is different from eating meat bought in the market: "you cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons". Such participation is incompatible with the Lord's Supper.
- *Practical rules (10:23-33).* Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience, since "the earth is the Lord's, and everything in it" (Psalm 24:1). If an invited unbeliever says that the meat has been offered in sacrifice, do not eat, for the sake of the conscience of the informant. Whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God, and seek the good of others (10:31-33).

**2. Assessment.**
- Paul agrees with the strong in theory (idols are nothing) but disagrees in practice, because love is the higher rule.
- He combines freedom with responsibility: freedom is used for the good of others.
- He forbids any participation in idol feasts, which are linked to idolatry and to division in the community.
- His teaching can be compared with the decree of the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15:29), which also mentions meat offered to idols, and shows that the matter was serious in the early church.
- It remains relevant to modern questions of conscience, culture and the limits of Christian freedom.

**Conclusion.** Paul teaches that food itself is not unclean, because idols are nothing, but that Christians must avoid idolatry, respect the conscience of the weak and act out of love for the glory of God.
